Abstract:

Neutron stars (NSs) provide a unique laboratory for studying matter at supra-nuclear densities and for probing physics beyond the Standard Model, particularly the elusive nature of dark matter (DM). This dissertation investigates how DM affects the internal structure, stability, and observable properties of NSs using a combination of relativistic mean field equations of state and both single-fluid and two-fluid frameworks. The study shows that the presence of DM generally softens the equation of state, reduces the maximum mass, and increases radial oscillation frequencies, while also modifying universal relations, tidal deformability, and gravitational-wave signatures in agreement with constraints from GW170817 and NICER observations. Extensions to rotating NSs demonstrate that DM significantly alters rotational deformation, while the inclusion of asymmetric DM and strong magnetic fields reveals complex degeneracies in their combined effects on stellar structure and stability. Overall, the results highlight that DM can leave measurable imprints on multiple neutron star observables, establishing NSs as powerful multimessenger probes for constraining the microphysical properties of dark matter.&nbsp
